questions.question: Let $\Lambda\ge0$ be a random annual risk rate and $L$ a stationary rating-class index, with finite second moments. Class frequency values $r_l$ minimise $\mathbb{E}[(\Lambda-r_L)^2]$. What quantity does $r_L$ predict?
options: The underlying annual risk rate of a member of the observed class.
The numerical class label of a member of the observed class.
The stationary probability of occupying the observed class.
The conditional squared error remaining in the observed class.

questions.question: For random risk rate $\Lambda$ with density $f_\Lambda$, let $\pi_l(\lambda)=\mathbb{P}(L=l\mid\Lambda=\lambda)$ for stationary class $L$. To price class $l$ by its conditional mean risk, which population receives more weight within that class?
options: Rates with larger $f_\Lambda(\lambda)$ alone.
Rates with larger $\pi_l(\lambda)$ alone.
Rates with larger $\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)$.
Every rate receives equal weight regardless of either factor.

questions.question: A class has optimal value $r_l=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid L=l]$, where $\Lambda$ is measured in claims per year. A positive base rate $\lambda_0$ has the same units. What distinguishes $r_l$ from a dimensionless premium relativity?
options: $r_l$ is dimensionless; $r_l\lambda_0$ is a rate.
$r_l$ is a rate; $\lambda_0/r_l$ is the intended class relativity.
$r_l$ is a class probability; dividing by $\lambda_0$ creates a rate.
$r_l$ is a rate; $r_l/\lambda_0$ is dimensionless.

questions.question: A stationary class $l$ has $\mathbb{P}(L=l)=0$. Other classes have positive probabilities and risk rate $\Lambda$ has finite second moment. How does changing the finite value assigned to this unused class affect $\mathbb{E}[(\Lambda-r_L)^2]$?
options: It changes the objective as much as changing any occupied class value.
It leaves the objective unchanged and does not identify that class value.
It forces the class value to equal the population mean rate.
It forces the class value to zero because the class probability is zero.

questions.question: Within one positive-probability class, the risk rate $\Lambda$ equals $0.1$ with probability $0.8$ and $0.6$ with probability $0.2$. Why does minimum squared-error pricing use the conditional mean rather than simply the most likely rate?
options: Squared deviations are minimised by the most frequent observed rate.
Squared deviations are minimised by the largest possible rate.
Squared deviations are minimised by the probability-weighted mean.
Squared deviations are minimised by ignoring the class probabilities.

questions.question: Stationary classes one and two have probabilities $0.75,0.25$ and optimal frequency values $r_1=0.1,r_2=0.5$ claims per year. What is the overall expected class frequency $\mathbb{E}[r_L]$?

Let $\Lambda$ be a random risk rate and $L$ the stationary class index. Under the restriction $r_l=a+bl$, suppose $\operatorname{Cov}(\Lambda,L)=0.06$ and $\operatorname{Var}(L)=0.3$. What is the minimum-MSE slope $b$?

For random risk rate $\Lambda$ and stationary class $L$, a minimum-MSE linear scale is $r_l=a+bl$. Suppose $\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]=0.4$, $\mathbb{E}[L]=2$ and optimal slope $b=0.1$. What is the intercept $a$?

For positive-probability class $l$, $r_l=\int_0^\infty\lambda\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\,/\,\int_0^\infty\pi_l(\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$, where $\pi_l$ is conditional stationary class probability and $f_\Lambda$ is the risk-rate density. What does the denominator represent?
options: The marginal probability $\mathbb{P}(L=l)$.
The population mean $\mathbb{E}[\Lambda]$.
The probability of class l at the population mean rate.
The sum of the numerical labels of occupied classes.

questions.question: Stationary class labels $1,2,3$ have positive probabilities and finite conditional risk second moments. No monotonicity restriction is imposed on the values minimising $\mathbb{E}[(\Lambda-r_L)^2]$. Must the optimal values increase with the class labels?
options: Yes; positive class probabilities force increasing conditional rates.
Yes; stationarity orders classes by their numerical labels.
No; they follow the conditional rate means, which need not be ordered.
No; all unconstrained optimal class values must be equal.

questions.question: A positive-probability stationary class is split into finer subclasses. Every child subclass has the same conditional risk mean as its parent, and all risk second moments are finite. How does this refinement affect the unconstrained minimum squared prediction error?
options: It strictly decreases because the number of labels increases.
It stays the same because every optimal prediction stays the same.
It increases because each child contains fewer members.
It becomes zero because every child can choose its own value.

questions.question: Risk rate $\Lambda$ is uniform on $(0,1)$, and stationary class $l$ has conditional occupancy $\pi_l(\lambda)=\lambda$. What is its optimal frequency value $r_l=\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid L=l]$?

Within an occupied stationary class, the risk rate has conditional mean $1$ and variance $0.09$. A proposed frequency value is $r=1.2$. What is the conditional MSE $\mathbb{E}[(\Lambda-r)^2\mid L=l]$?
A minimum-MSE linear frequency scale for stationary label $L$ is $r_L=0.4+0.2L$, with $\operatorname{Var}(L)>0$. Relabel the same classes by $J=L+10$. Which scale in $J$ gives identical predictions?

Two stationary class systems classify the same finite-second-moment risk population. System B has more occupied classes than system A, but B is not a refinement of A: some A classes are mixed together in B. Is lower unconstrained minimum MSE guaranteed for B?
options: Yes; the number of occupied classes alone orders minimum MSE.
Yes; both systems have the same unconditional risk mean.
No; any change of class system must increase minimum MSE.
No; more labels can still discard risk information retained by A.

questions.question: An occupied stationary class has non-negative risk rate with finite conditional mean but infinite conditional second moment. Proposed class frequency values are finite constants. Why does a finite mean alone not justify claiming a unique finite-MSE optimum there?
options: The class conditional mean must equal its second moment.
Every finite prediction can still have infinite squared error.
A finite class prediction necessarily makes squared error finite.
The class occupancy probability cancels the infinite second moment.

questions.question: Stationary label $L$ is uniform on $\{1,2,3\}$ and risk rate $\Lambda=(L-2)^2$. Thus $\operatorname{Cov}(\Lambda,L)=0$. How do the optimal linear and unconstrained class frequency scales compare?
options: Linear prediction is 2/3 with MSE 2/9; unconstrained MSE is zero.
Both predictions are 2/3 with MSE 2/9 because covariance is zero.
Linear prediction is zero with MSE 2/3; unconstrained MSE is zero.
Both scales have zero MSE because the rate is a function of the class.

questions.question: Every policy occupies stationary class $L=2$. Risk rate $\Lambda$ equals $0.1$ or $0.3$ with equal probabilities. Under $r_L=a+bL$, what does minimum-MSE fitting determine when $\operatorname{Var}(L)=0$?
options: Uniquely a=0.2 and b=0 by the covariance-over-variance formula.
Uniquely a=0 and b=0.2 because the mean risk rate is 0.2.
Only a+2b=0.2; many coefficient pairs give the same optimal prediction.
Only a+2b=0.4 because there are two possible risk rates.
